attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the type of data to be shared with the user to improve the User Experience (UX) of the mini golf project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to display custom pixel art screens throughout the project and to share data with the user?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to display custom pixel art screens throughout the project and to share data with the user in this third Build activity. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the mini golf code.
steps.instructions:
This is the third of three Build activities where you will create a mini golf project! 


Notice that the code from the Build 2 activity has already been added into the JavaScript editor. In this third Build activity, you’ll use that code to design User Interface (UI) features to add the finishing touches to the mini golf project. In this Build activity, you’ll design multiple splash screens and share data with the user to enhance the User Experience (UX) of the project! 


What kind of information might the user want to see at the beginning of the project? What information might they want to know at the end of each level?

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare the 2 text sprites under // project initialization so that they can be accessed throughout the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will the strokes, holeNum, and strokeCount variables be used for in the project?

❓ What arguments might be passed to each text sprite function in the displayHoleNum and displayStrokes functions to improve the project’s User Interface (UI)?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that variables are a great way to collect and share data with the user in a project. In this example, the number of strokes taken per level will be displayed by the strokeCount text sprite, and the holeNum will display the current hole number to the user. These values will update throughout the project, keeping the user up to date with the current status of their playing.
steps.instructions:
Continue the mini golf project by displaying the hole number and stroke count on screen!


One way to improve the user’s experience (UX) is to give the user immediate feedback after each stroke attempt! 


Under the existing variable code below // project initialization, declare a strokes variable set to 0 to keep track of the number of times the user has hit the ball. The existing levelNum variable will be used to update the current hole on screen.


Add the arcade-text extension to the project. Use textsprite.create to declare 2 blank text sprites, holeNum and strokeCount, and set their background color. 


Define 2 functions below the existing createStatusBar function that will display the hole and stroke count data, and name them:  displayHoleNum and displayStrokes.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use convertToText inside the  setText functions of both function definitions to change the value of the levelNum and strokes variables into a string that can be displayed to the user?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the convertToText functions be placed to convert the number values of the levelNum and strokes variables to strings?

❓ Where should the displayHoleNum and displayStrokes functions be called?

❓ Do the 2 text sprites appear as intended on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to place the convertToText functions inside the parentheses of the setText functions. Then type the levelNum and strokes variables inside the parentheses of the convertToText functions.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider why the flagIcon and clubIcon image assets should be used as the icons for each text sprite, and how that communicates the value’s purpose to the user. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out different sizes, colors, and borders for the text sprites so that they stand out on screen. Remind the ninja to set the background color for each text sprite, to create contrast against the background. Prompt the ninja to test out the position of the text sprites, then update the coordinates to make sure they are visible and out of the way on screen.
steps.instructions:
Set the position and image icons of the hole number and stroke count on screen!


Inside the displayHoleNum and displayStrokes functions, use the setText and  convertToText functions to display the value of the levelNum and strokes variables in the corresponding function definition. 


Use the flagIcon and clubIcon image assets to set each text sprite’s icon. Place each text sprite in opposite upper corners of the screen, use a sprite flag to set the position relative to the camera. Then, set the max font height and border of each text sprite.


Call the functions whenever a 2D tilemap is displayed. Notice where the text sprites appear, then update each sprite’s properties, as needed.


Click ▶ to see the text sprites displayed on the 2D tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the convertToText function to convert the number value of strokes to a string that can be displayed by the strokeCount text sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the strokes variable be updated each time the A button is released, rather than pressed or repeated?

❓ Where should the code to reset the strokes variable be placed inside the onOverlapTile event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to think through the placement of the code to update the value of the strokes variable. Its value should increase by 1 once the A button is released, because that signals when the ball is actually hit (rather than when it is pressed). If it were placed in the A button repeated event, the variable’s value would increase while the button is held down, resulting in a far larger increase than 1.

💡 The code to reset the strokes variable should be placed inside the second after function before the callScene function call, inside the onOverlapTile event.
steps.instructions:
Update the value displayed on screen when the user hits the golf ball!


Add code to increase the value of the strokes variable each time the A button is released. Then, update the string displayed by the strokeCount sprite so that the current value is displayed on the screen.


Then, reset strokes to 0, 2000 ms after the ball has landed in the hole at the end of each level. Update the value before the top down tilemap is displayed.


Click ▶ to test the updated stroke count code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set each text sprite’s Invisible sprite flag to true when the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile and to false when in the displayHoleNum and displayStrokes function definitions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When should holeNum and strokeCount text sprites Invisible sprite flag be turned on and off?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja test out their code to make sure they’ve set the Invisible sprite flag for each text sprite on and off in the correct locations, so that the text sprites disappear when the top down tilemap is displayed.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The hole number and stroke count text sprites still appear when the Player sprite returns to the top down tilemap!


Use the Invisible sprite flag to only show the holeNum and strokeCount text sprites when the 2D tilemap is displayed. 


Add code inside the displayHoleNum and displayStrokes function definitions to make the text sprites visible when the 2D level begins. Make the text sprites invisible when the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile to end each level.


Click ▶ to test when the text sprites are visible on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you draw letters at the top of each column on the scoreCardImage asset, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How you might you design a scoreCardImage asset? 

❓ What tools can you use to make sure 3 columns are created of equal size?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the various tools in the paint editor at their disposal. They can use the line tool to draw straight lines to divide each tile, updating the thickness of the line as needed. Additionally, prompt the ninja to use the coordinates at the bottom left side of the screen to space out each column evenly. The marquee tool can also be used to reposition any of the lines or text to organize the space on the image asset. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to recall the pixel art strategies that they’ve already learned when drawing the titles for each column. They might begin to casually draw each letter, then go back and remove jaggies as needed to make each letter clear and stand out on the image. Encourage the ninja to think about what colors might be used to complement or contrast with each other.
steps.instructions:
Use a scorecard to keep track of the user’s score throughout the mini golf course!


Another way to improve UX is to share a summary of the level with the user, after a level has been completed. Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and create a new scoreCardImage asset. Resize the canvas to 80 x 60, so that the image will fill a large part of the screen when displayed.


Use the line tool to create 3 distinct columns in the image. Then, use the paint tool to draw a title for each column: Hole, Par, and Score. Use colors that will make the text pop on screen.


Leave plenty of space underneath each title so that text sprites can be added to fill the scorecard throughout the project. The scorecard will display values to represent the current hole number, the par number value (or the base number of strokes it takes to complete a hole), and the user’s actual number of tries used to complete the hole.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the time parameter in the after function inside the onOverlapTile event, so that the user has enough time to view the scorecard before it disappears?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the createScoreCard function call be placed in the onOverlapTile event?

❓ Why should the Scorecard sprite be destroyed before the top down tilemap is displayed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The createScoreCard function call should be placed before the second after function inside the onOverlapTile event. The ninja should update the time parameter in this function so that there is enough time to view the score card image, before the top down tilemap is displayed.
steps.instructions:
Display the scorecard at the end of each level!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then define a createScoreCard function. 


Inside the function definition, create a scoreCard sprite with its image set to the scoreCardImage asset. Change its kind to TextSprite. Use the RelativeToCamera sprite flag to display the image in the middle of the screen, regardless of the camera’s position.


Call the function once the Ball sprite has disappeared into the hole at the end of each level. Destroy all TextSpite sprites before the top down tilemap is displayed.


Click ▶ to view the scorecard after completing each hole!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a yOffset value with a spacing value, multiplied by the counter variable i to set each text sprite’s y-position?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used inside the textsprite.create function to convert a number value to a string?

❓ What values might be added and multiplied in the setPosition function to space out each TextSprite in the “Hole” column of the scorecard?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the convertToText function should be used inside the textsprite.create function to convert an element from the levelCount array to a string.

💡 Have the ninja tinker with the size, position, and color of the TextSprites to make sure they are clearly legible on the scorecard image. Remind the ninja that multiples of 5 and 8 can be passed to the setMaxFontHeight function, to update the size of the text. Prompt the ninja to use the for loop’s counter variable when setting the position of the TextSprites.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider what values are needed to properly space out the y-positions of each text sprite. The spacing between sprites should be calculated first, which may be slightly larger than the text sprite’s height. This value should be multiplied by the loop’s counter variable i inside parentheses. Then, the initial y-position (or the yOffset) of the first text sprite should be added to the equation. The code might look like:

textSprite.setPosition(50, 50 + (i * 15))
steps.instructions:
Use text sprites to display the hole numbers on the scorecard!


Under // project initialization, declare a levelCount array. Store the numbers 1, 2, and 3 in the array to represent each hole of the mini golf course.


Inside the createScoreCard function definition, use a for loop to create a text sprite for each element of the levelCount array. Above the loop, add a comment that tells what the for loop will do, such as: // creates hole number text sprite. 


Inside the loop, be sure to set the text color, so that the text sprite is visible on the scorecard. Use the setPosition function to place each text sprite in the left “Hole” column of the scorecard. Remember to space out the text sprites by adding a yOffset value, too.


Then, change the sprites’ kinds to TextSprite, tinker with the font height and the z-property, and set the RelativeToCamera sprite flag on.


Click ▶ to see each hole number displayed on the scorecard! Update the positioning and size of the text sprites so that they fit the space of the scorecard image.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you playtest each level to identify the par score to add to the scorecard?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does “par” mean in mini golf? What does it mean to score above or below “par”?

❓ What is the difficulty of each hole on the mini golf course? What values should be placed in the parScores array for each hole?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that par represents the base number of strokes it takes to complete each hole. Have the ninja test out each hole a few times to measure its difficulty, making note of how many strokes were required. Once the difficulty has been assessed, number values should be added to the parScores array to reflect this.
steps.instructions:
Add the par scores to the scorecard!


Under // project initialization, declare a parScores array. Store 3 numbers in the array to represent the par scores, or the base number of strokes it takes to complete each hole. Keep in mind the difficulty of each hole when determining the par score for that level.


Then, copy the for loop used to create the hole number text sprites and the comment above it inside the createScoreCard function definition and paste it below. 


Update the array used in the textsprite.create function to make sure the correct values are accessed. Then, update the x-position of the text sprites so that the par scores appear in the middle “Par'' column of the scorecard. Update the code comment to describe what the second for loop does.


Click ▶ to see each par score number displayed on the scorecard!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you push the value of the strokes variable to the totalStrokeArray in the onOverlapTile event before the scorecard is displayed and the variable is reset?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbols are used to declare an empty array?

❓ How is the strokes variable used to keep track of the number of strokes the user has completed throughout the game?

❓Do the numbers appear as expected in each column on the scorecard image? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the formatting needed to create an empty array. The keyword let should be typed followed by the name of the array and a colon :. Then, the array type (number) and a pair of brackets should be added, followed by an assignment operator and another pair of brackets. The code should look like:

let totalStrokeArray: number[] = []

💡 Walk the ninja through how values stored in the various variables and arrays of the project keep track of user data and improve the overall user experience of the project by creating realistic features. In this example, the strokes variable stores the total number of strokes needed to complete each hole. This value is pushed to the totalStrokeArray after each hole and reset to 0 for the next. At the end of the course, the totalStrokeArray will contain 3 values that can be totaled and shared with the user.

💡 Encourage the user to test out the scorecard image code to make sure that numbers are spaced out correctly and appear as intended on the image. In the next step, the ninja will add a sprite flag to make sure the values in the “Score” column appear correctly.
steps.instructions:
Add the user’s stroke count in each hole to the scorecard!


Under // project initialization, declare an empty number array called totalStrokeArray. This will be used to store the user’s stroke count after each level is completed.


Then, copy the for loop used to create the par score text sprites inside the createScoreCard function definition and paste it below. 


Run the for loop while the counter variable is less than the length of the totalStrokeArray. Then, update the array used in the textsprite.create function and the x-position of the text sprites so that each stroke amount appears in the right “Score” column of the scorecard. Update the code comment to describe what the third for loop does, too.


Then, use the push function after each hole is completed to update the totalStrokeArray with the number of tries it took the user.


Click ▶ to try and use fewer strokes than the par score to complete each hole!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Ball sprite’s GhostThroughTiles sprite flag to false when 2 is passed to the callScene function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the GhostThroughTiles sprite flag needed? How does it solve this bug?

❓ When should the Ball sprite’s GhostThroughTiles sprite flag be turned back off?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the scorecard code, if they have not done so already, to notice what happens when the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile asset. 

💡 The GhostThroughTiles sprite flag prevents an overlap event from being triggered when a sprite overlaps a specific tile. As a result, this allows only 1 value to be pushed to the totalStrokeArray, rather than running all of the code inside the onOverlapTile event while the Ball sprite overlaps the holeTile.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The score column on the scorecard is displaying too many numbers because the Ball sprite continues to overlap the holeTile. 


Use the GhostThroughTiles sprite flag to stop the overlap event between the Ball sprite and the holeTile asset, once it’s occurred.


Be sure to reset the Ball sprite’s sprite flag when the 2D tilemap is displayed to start each level.


Click ▶ to see the current level’s stroke count displayed in the score column of the scorecard!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a golf-themed splashScreen image asset with enough space to display the hole number, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might you include in your golf-themed splashScreen image asset?

❓ What tools from the paint editor might be used to design the large image asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use all of the pixel art skills that they’ve already learned about when designing their golf-themed splashScreen image asset. In the paint editor, they can use the paint, fill, erase, and marquee tools to adjust the visuals on the image asset and fill in any extra space. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider where shadows might be present, where to remove jaggies, and how to use dithering to enhance the image asset.
steps.instructions:
Design a splash screen to announce each hole to the user!


Another way to improve UX in a game is to show the user what level they are entering. In some games, this time is needed to load all of the assets. This also gives users a few seconds to prepare for the game to begin!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and create a new splashScreen image asset. Resize the canvas so that the image will fill a large part of the screen when displayed.


Use the fill, paint, and line tools to design a golf themed image to be displayed at the beginning of each level. Leave enough solid space in the image where a large text sprite can be added to display the hole number.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the splashScreen function after the levelNum variable is updated inside the 2 onOverlapTile events?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What variable should be used to display the current hole number to the user?

❓ Where should the splashScreen function be called in the 2 onOverlapTile events that begin the 2D tilemap levels?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the levelNum variable stores the current hole number throughout the project and should be joined with a string to create on screen text.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider why the splashScreen function be called after the levelNum variable is updated inside the 2 onOverlapTile events. After the Player sprite overlaps each tile to trigger the beginning of the level, the levelNum variable is updated with the next hole’s number. If the function is called prior to this, then the wrong value will be displayed on the splash screen.
steps.instructions:
Display the splashScreen image at the beginning of each level!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then define a splashScreen function. 


Inside the function definition, create a sprite with its image set to the splashScreen asset. Then, create a text sprite that tells the user the current hole number. Set the font color, position, and size of the text sprite, too.


Use the after function to destroy the splash image and text sprites after a certain amount of time.


Call the function inside the onOverlapTile events to begin the 2D tilemap levels.


Click ▶ to test the splash screen code.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an AND operator && inside the conditions of the A button pressed, released, and repeated events to check if the level has started?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When should levelStarted be set to true or false throughout the game?

❓ What symbols should be used to check for multiple conditions in each A button event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that Boolean variables are a great way to keep track of game conditions in a project. In this example, the levelStarted variable is used to keep track of whether the splash screen and score card images are currently displayed, and if so, to prevent sprite movement while viewing.
steps.instructions:
Prevent the Ball, Player, and status bar movement while the splash screen and scorecard images are displayed on the 2D tilemap.


Under // project initialization, declare a levelStarted variable to keep track of when the movement can occur on the 2D tilemap. Set the variable to false at the beginning of the project.


Update the value of the variable once the splash screen has been destroyed and again at the end of the level.


Update the A button pressed, released, and repeated events to check whether levelStarted is true before allowing sprite movement.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the A button is pressed and held while on the 2D tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you position the title text strategically in both the image and animation assets so that it aligns with the background image, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might you include in your homeScreen background image asset?

❓ What tools from the paint editor might be used to design the large image assets?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use all of the pixel art skills that they’ve already learned about when designing their homeScreen background image asset. In the paint editor, they can use the paint, fill, erase, and marquee tools as well as the different brush sizes to adjust the visuals on the image asset. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider where shadows might be present, where to remove jaggies, and how to use dithering to enhance the image asset.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider why it might be useful to create separate assets for the background image and the title text, and why only the text should be added to the animation asset. This will make it easier to edit and update the text once finalized, rather than interfering with the background image.
steps.instructions:
Design a home screen for the project!


Another way to improve UX is to add an engaging and exciting home screen. This gives the user a hint to what the project will be about, and can also showcase specific visual assets.


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and create a homeScreen background image asset to be displayed when the user begins the project. Use the tools in the paint editor to create an engaging background image that will immediately capture the user’s attention.


Next, create a homeScreenText image asset that is also the size of the screen. On this image asset, use the paint tool (and the various brush sizes) to draw the name of the project to be displayed in front of the background image asset. Consider how to make the text pop on screen by tinkering with line thickness as well as highlight and shadow colors. 


Finally, copy the homeScreenText image asset and paste it into the first frame of a titleAnim animation asset. Use the show previous frame, duplicate, and marquee tools to animate the title and create an engaging opening scene for the user.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you make any updates to the assets or position code to make the home screen look the way you intended?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the titleText sprite be positioned on screen?

❓ Why is it useful to add code comments within each condition in the callScene function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to test the position of the titleText sprite and the corresponding animation to make sure they appear correctly. Encourage the ninja to make updates to the code and the image/animation assets to enhance the background image visual on screen.

💡 Remind the ninja that code comments are useful for organizing code and remembering what certain sections do. Because the scene number doesn’t always imply what the scene represents, it’s useful to have a text reminder in the code to recall what each chunk of code will lead to.
steps.instructions:
Display the home screen at the beginning of the project!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a condition that checks if sceneNum is equal to 0 inside the callScene function definition. 


Add a // home screen comment inside the condition, then set the background image to the homeScreen image asset. 


Below, create a sprite with its image set to the homeScreenText image asset. Set the position of the image so that it appears in the middle of the screen; tinker with the coordinate values so that it aligns with the background image. Animate the sprite with the titleAnim animation asset.


Update the function call under // project start, then click ▶ to test the home screen code.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player and Ball sprites’ Invisible sprite flags to true when 0 is passed to the callScene function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When should the Player and Ball sprite be set to invisible?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the opening scene of the project. Does the image appear correctly? Is the text correctly positioned? Do the Player and Ball sprites disappear as expected?
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player and Ball sprites still appear when the home screen is displayed.


Use the Invisible sprite flag to hide the Player sprite if sceneNum is equal to 0 when the callScene function is called. Cut the existing code that turns the Ball sprite’s Invisible sprite flag if sceneNum is equal to 1 and paste it into the condition that checks if sceneNum is equal to 0.


Click ▶ to test the home screen display without the Player and Ball sprites present.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add code to destroy the title sprite then display a set of directions when 0 is passed to the callScene function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might be useful for the user to know when beginning the project? 

❓ What coordinates should be used in the printDialog function to position the direction text correctly on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the opening scene of the project to make sure that everything appears correctly. Prompt the ninja to review the printDialog function parameters to set the appropriate values, then test out the direction code and update the position coordinates to make sure the text is fully legible on screen.
steps.instructions:
Add directions to the project introduction!


A very important part of UX design is including directions which tell the user how to navigate around the game. Add text that explains to the user how to move around the golf course, which buttons to press to hit the golf ball, and what the status bar represents!


Under // project initialization, declare a directions array. Inside, store several strings that tell the user how to play the game. Be sure to include what buttons to press, how to navigate between tilemaps, and what the user’s goal is.


Then, use the after function to destroy the title sprite once the user has had a chance to view the project title and animation. 


Add the arcade-story extension to the project. Use a for loop and a printDialog function to display each string in the directions array on screen.


Once all of the directions have been shown, display the top down tilemap on screen.


Click ▶ to test the project’s introduction sequence.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace the gameOver function with callScene(3) in the onOverlapTile event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might you include in your endScreen background image asset?

❓ What tools from the paint editor might be used to design the large image asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use all of the pixel art skills that they’ve already learned about when designing their endScreen background image asset. In the paint editor, they can use the paint, fill, erase, and marquee tools as well as the different brush sizes to adjust the visuals on the image asset. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider where shadows might be present, where to remove jaggies, and how to use dithering to enhance the image asset.
steps.instructions:
Design the project’s ending sequence!


Last but not least, just like credits in a movie, a great game ends with an ending sequence! Improve the final part of the game by adding a summary of the score. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and create an endScreenImage background image asset to be displayed at the end of the project. Use the tools in the paint editor to create a background image that will appear behind the scorecard.


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a condition that checks if sceneNum is equal to 3 inside the callScene function definition. 


Add an // end screen comment inside the condition, then update the background image and use the blankTilemap asset to reset the tilemap.


Destroy both Player and Ball sprites so that they do not appear on the end screen. Then call the createScoreCard function to show the user their final scores.


When the Player sprite overlaps the endTile asset on the top down tilemap, call the end scene instead of immediately ending the game.


Click ▶ to test the project’s ending sequence.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an addition assignment operator += to add the current value of strokes to the totalStrokeCount variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When should the totalStrokeCount variable be updated in the project?

❓ Which symbol should be used to add the current value of strokes to the totalStrokeCount variable?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to identify where to place the totalStrokeCount += strokes code in the onOverlapTile function. This should be done before the strokes variable is reset and before the top down tilemap is displayed.
steps.instructions:
Use a variable to calculate the user’s final score!


Under // project initialization, declare a totalStrokeCount variable set to 0. This will be used to store the user’s actual score throughout the project.


At the end of each level, update the totalStrokeCount variable before the strokes variable is reset.

steps.hints: ❓Did you check if the user’s totalStrokeCount was greater than, equal to, or less than the total goal score when 3 is passed to the callScene function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it necessary to find the total par scores before presenting the final data to the user?

❓ What math operators should be used inside the printDialog function to calculate how many strokes greater or less than the total par score the user scored?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the par scores are stored in the parScores array as individual values for each hole and need to be totaled to compare it with the user’s final score.

💡 Walk through the logic needed to present the correct message to the user at the end of the project. Prompt the ninja to identify where greater than, equals, less than, subtraction, and addition signs are needed to present the correct data to the user.
steps.instructions:
Tell the user how they performed at the end of the project!


Add an after function after the scorecard is displayed on the end screen to share a message with the user about how they did on the course. 


First, calculate the sum of the par scores listed on the scorecard to identify the total goal score for the game. Then, use several printDialog functions and if/else if conditions to share the user’s total score and whether that amount was greater than, equal to, or less than the total goal score. Use math symbols and the totalStrokeCount variable to share specific data with the user.


Add a nested after function, then play a closing melody and end the game once all of the messages have been shared with the user. Add additional melodies throughout the project to add to the user’s experience, too!


Click ▶ to test out the entire game, then see how the final score compares with the goal score.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you make additional updates to the project’s assets or code to further improve the User Experience (UX)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What else could be added or modified to further improve and customize this project?

❓ What is something you used to create this project that could be applied to your Adventure project?

❓ What other strategies might you use to debug an error in the code with a project of this size?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Once the ninja has completed the project, invite them to debrief about the process. What did they feel confident in? Which parts were hard? What else might they change about the process? Encourage the ninja to reflect on the size of this project, emphasizing that it required 3 Build activities to create. With this in mind, they will create an Adventure project of a similar size and complexity to demonstrate the concepts that they’ve learned during this level. Prompt the ninja to identify 2-3 things that they used to create the mini golf project that they plan to incorporate into their Adventure project.

💡 Encourage the ninja to playtest their project with other ninjas as well. Provide sentence starters to the ninjas to encourage both positive and constructive feedback, then work with the ninja to identify pieces of feedback to incorporate into their code.

💡 One useful debugging strategy for large projects is to use the sayText function, especially to check that variables and arrays are updating correctly throughout the project. Review the ninja’s code together, looking for areas that could be improved, then insert the sayText function to test the source of the issue.
steps.instructions:
Playtest, debug, and refactor the project!


This project took 3 different Build activities to complete and there are a lot of moving pieces within it! 


Playtest the project several times and think about what’s working well and what could be improved. Show the project to another ninja or Code Sensei for additional feedback. Make any necessary updates to further improve the User Experience (UX) of the game.


During playtesting, try to identify any actions that seem to work sometimes, but aren’t always consistent. Review the code in the editor to debug what the issue might be. Don’t forget to comment out code or use the sayText function to “say” the value of a variable, to test a small chunk of code at a time.


Finally, look through the code in the editor to identify any functions that are used repeatedly throughout the project and locate areas that can be refactored to make the code more efficient. Try to trim down any code that might not be needed at the end of the project.

subgroups.introduction: Complete the mini golf project by designing User Interface (UI) features to enhance the User Experience (UX) of the project!

validationItems.text: Use functions and text sprites to display the hole number and stroke count on screen. Update each value throughout the project.
Create a large scorecard image asset that uses functions and text sprites to display the hole number, par score, and user score at the end of each level.
Use sprite flags to set when sprites are visible on screen and when they trigger tile overlap events.
Create a large splash screen image asset that uses functions and a text sprite to display the hole number before each level.
Use a Boolean variable to keep track of whether the level has begun and update sprite movement accordingly.

Create 2 large image assets and 1 animation asset to create an engaging background image and title screen for the beginning of the project. Use a function to display and sequence the assets on screen.
Use the timer and story extensions to sequence and display project instructions stored in an array.
Create a large background image asset to be displayed at the end of the project.
Use a function, variables, math operators, and the story extension to share the user’s final score at the end of the project.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Red Belt! In this level, you’ll apply your previous learning by creating a complex mini golf project in JavaScript across 3 different Build activities. There is no pre-assessment Quest activity for this level, so click “Start Level” to begin! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:
